\chapter{When}
\label{ch:ta-when}
\hlchaptermodality{79}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask when, point at a time already named, and say that two things happen together.}

Complete TA-C79-when-clause and say the three time-words, then a when-clause.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[eppōdu]{\ta{எப்போது} (eppōdu) — when?}

\label{lesson:TA-C79-when-question}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{so, therefore}. Then say: tea for you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{எப்போது}}
\textbf{\ta{எப்போது}} (\emph{eppōdu}) — \textquotedblleft{}when?\textquotedblright{}

You have had \textbf{\ta{இப்போது}}, \textquotedblleft{}now\textquotedblright{}, since chapter forty-eight, and you have had the pattern behind it since chapter forty: \textbf{i-} for near, \textbf{a-} for far, \textbf{e-} for a question.

So this word was already half yours:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{இப்போது}} & \emph{ippōdu} & now — this time \\
\textbf{\ta{எப்போது}} & \emph{eppōdu} & when? — which time \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The shared piece is \textbf{\ta{போது}}, a word meaning \emph{a time, an occasion}. Change only the front and you have walked from a statement to a question, exactly as \ta{இங்கே} walked to \ta{எங்கே}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{எப்போது} \ta{வேண்டும்}?} — \textquotedblleft{}When do you want it?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The question word for time, and the small word \ta{போது} that sits inside it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{eppōdu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ippōdu}, then \emph{eppōdu} — the statement, then the question
  \item \emph{Ask:} \emph{eppōdu vēṇḍum?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{adaṉāl}, then say \emph{uṅgaḷukkāga}, then ask \emph{eppōdu?}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{-um}, \emph{kaḷam} and \emph{ēṉ} — three distances back — then say when one of them happens
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the piece these two words share, and what does it mean? (\textbf{\ta{போது} — a time.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[appōdu]{\ta{அப்போது} (appōdu) — then, at that time}

\label{lesson:TA-C79-then}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{for you}. Then ask \emph{when?}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அப்போது}}
\textbf{\ta{அப்போது}} (\emph{appōdu}) — \textquotedblleft{}then, at that time\textquotedblright{}.

The third seat was empty and now it is filled:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{இப்போது}} & \emph{ippōdu} & now \\
\textbf{\ta{அப்போது}} & \emph{appōdu} & then \\
\textbf{\ta{எப்போது}} & \emph{eppōdu} & when? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Near, far, question — the same three fronts you first met on \ta{இங்கே}, \ta{அங்கே}, \ta{எங்கே}.

\emph{Then} in Tamil means a time somebody has already named. It looks backwards, the way \ta{அதனால்} does, and for the same reason: both begin on the \textbf{a-} that means \emph{that one, over there}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{நாளை}. \ta{அப்போது} \ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}.} — \textquotedblleft{}Tomorrow. Tell me then.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A complete set of three, from a pattern you were given nearly forty chapters ago.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{appōdu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} all three in order — \emph{ippōdu, appōdu, eppōdu}
  \item \emph{Notice:} the front that means \emph{that one}, in \ta{அப்போது} and in \ta{அதனால்}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{uṅgaḷukkāga}, then ask \emph{eppōdu?}, then answer \emph{appōdu}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{aṟuvaṭai}, read \textbf{\ta{பாலும்}} and say \emph{ēṉeṉṟāl} — three distances back — then say when one of them happens
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why can \ta{அப்போது} never open a conversation? (\textbf{Because \emph{a-} points at a time somebody has already named.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eppōdu]{\ta{எப்போது} — the doubled letter, read across a seam}

\label{lesson:TA-W34-read-eppothu}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: say \emph{now}, \emph{then}, \emph{when?} in that order.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{எப்போது} — one letter, twice, on either side of a \ta{புள்ளி}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{எ}} & \emph{e} & the free-standing short e, because the word opens on it \\
\textbf{\ta{ப்}} & \emph{p} & \ta{ப} with a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}} \\
\textbf{\ta{போ}} & \emph{pō} & \ta{ப} with the wrapping \textbf{\ta{ோ}} sign \\
\textbf{\ta{து}} & \emph{du} & \ta{த} with the \textbf{\ta{ு}} sign \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{எ} · \ta{ப்} · \ta{போ} · \ta{து} $\to$ \ta{எப்போது}}
\end{quote}

The middle is the shape you first read in \textbf{\ta{சட்டை}}: the same letter written twice, the first one wearing a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}} and leaning on the second. Here it is \ta{ப}, and the doubling is exactly what makes the \emph{pp} you hear.

Read the seam and the word divides itself: \textbf{\ta{எ}} is the question front from chapter forty, and \textbf{\ta{போது}} is the time-word. \textbf{\ta{அப்போது}} is the same page with one letter changed at the start.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{எ}} — then \textbf{\ta{ப்}} — then \textbf{\ta{போ}} — then \textbf{\ta{து}}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}}, then \textbf{\ta{அப்போது}}
  \item \emph{Point to:} the two \ta{ப} shapes, and say which one carries no vowel
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{eppōdu?}, then answer \emph{appōdu}, then read \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{-um … -um illai}, say \emph{kuḍi} and read \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}} — three distances back — then say when one of them happens
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}}. Which one letter would you change to read \emph{then} instead? (\textbf{The first — \ta{எ} becomes \ta{அ}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-um pōdu]{-\ta{உம்} \ta{போது} — when one thing happens, so does another}

\label{lesson:TA-C79-when-clause}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}}. Then say \emph{then, at that time}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: the time-word does the joining}]
\textbf{\ta{எப்போது}} asks about a time. \textbf{\ta{போது}} on its own can pin one, and when a verb stands in front of it the whole thing becomes \emph{when that happens}.

The verb takes \textbf{-\ta{உம்}} first:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{வா}} $\to$ \textbf{\ta{வரும்}} $\to$ \textbf{\ta{வரும்} \ta{போது}} — \textquotedblleft{}at the coming time\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}when {[}you{]} come\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{நீங்கள்} \ta{வரும்} \ta{போது}, \ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{nīṅgaḷ varum pōdu, solluṅgaḷ.} — \textquotedblleft{}When you come, tell me.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Two things happening at once, held together by a word that means \emph{time}. No word for \emph{when} is needed, because \ta{போது} already is one.

One warning, because it would otherwise mislead you. The \textbf{-\ta{உம்}} here is \textbf{not} the joining ending from chapter seventy-four. That one sat on nouns and meant \emph{and}. This one sits on verbs and marks a happening. Same two letters, two different jobs — and the word in front of them tells you which.

Everyday speech runs it together and clips it, so you will hear \emph{varumbōdu} as one word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The last of this chapter's three: a time you ask about, a time you point at, and a time you build out of a verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{varum pōdu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nīṅgaḷ varum pōdu, solluṅgaḷ}
  \item \emph{Separate:} say \emph{pālum} and then \emph{varum} — the same ending, two different jobs
  \item \emph{Recall:} answer \emph{appōdu}, then read \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}}, then say the whole \emph{varum pōdu} line
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{-ā}, \emph{naḍa} and \emph{adaṉāl} — three distances back — then say when one of them happens
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two words end in -\ta{உம்}: \textbf{\ta{பாலும்}} and \textbf{\ta{வரும்}}. What tells them apart? (\textbf{What they sit on — a naming word joins, a doing word marks a happening.})
\end{tcolorbox}
